01 · Adam optimizer · The problem

One learning rate can't fit every weight

Gradient descent moves every weight by the same learning rate × its gradient. When some directions are steep and others flat, no single learning rate works for both.

The steep direction sets the limit

Above lr = 0.1, SGD diverges here: the steep weight overshoots further every step.

So the flat direction crawls

At lr = 0.095, each step closes only 5% of the remaining distance along the valley.

Noise makes it worse

Minibatch gradients jitter, so the real path zig-zags even more.

Adam fixes this

It averages the direction (momentum) and gives every weight its own step size.

Toy loss L = ½ (0.5·w1² + 20·w2²), simulated, 25 steps each. SGD lr 0.095; Adam α 0.45, β1 0.9, β2 0.999.

Explain

  • Gradient descent: θ ← θ − η·g. One number η for every weight.
  • On this valley the steep weight has curvature 20 and the flat one 0.5 (condition number 40). Stability needs η < 2/20 = 0.1. At that η the flat weight shrinks by only (1 − 0.095·0.5) ≈ 0.95 per step, so SGD needs roughly 40× more steps than the steep direction alone would.
  • Real networks are much worse: embeddings, layer norms and output layers see gradients that differ by orders of magnitude, and rare features get gradients only now and then.
  • Adam's two ideas map onto the two failures: momentum cancels the zig-zag (slide 2), per-weight scaling lets the flat weight take full-size steps (slide 3).

Honest caveat

Adam rescales each weight separately (a diagonal preconditioner). It fixes a valley that is aligned with the axes, like this one. If the valley were rotated 45°, per-weight scaling would help much less: that needs full second-order information (Newton, Shampoo, SOAP).

Check yourself

  • Why can't we just raise SGD's learning rate to speed up the flat direction? Because the steep direction then overshoots and diverges.

02 · Idea 1 · Momentum

Idea 1: step along the average gradient

Keep a running average of past gradients. Directions that flip sign cancel out; directions that agree keep their size, with less noise.

: an exponential moving average over roughly the last gradients.
Recent gradients weigh most; old ones fade by ×0.9 per step.

Steep weight w2: the gradient flips sign

The average falls below 0.2 while the raw gradient is still above 2. The zig-zag cancels.

Flat weight w1: the gradient keeps its sign

The average stays near −1 and is much smoother. Steady progress along the valley.

bars: raw gradient gline: average m (with the slide-4 correction)

20 simulated steps. Steep: g = ±4·0.97^t. Flat: g = −1 + noise (sd 0.35, seed 3).

Explain

  • Unrolled, the average is a weighted sum: m_t = (1−β1)·Σ β1^(t−i)·g_i. Weights 0.1, 0.09, 0.081, … add up to 1, so keeps the gradient's units and size.
  • Alternating signs: +4 and −3.9 nearly cancel in the sum, so ≈ 0 along the steep weight. No more bouncing between the walls.
  • Consistent signs: the average keeps the full value, and independent noise shrinks: its standard deviation drops by √((1−β1)/(1+β1)) ≈ 0.23 for β1 = 0.9.
  • Physics picture: a heavy ball rolling downhill. It keeps its velocity along the valley floor and ignores small bumps.

Deeper

  • Classic SGD momentum sums gradients (v = μv + g), which grows the step by 1/(1−μ). Adam's version averages instead, so the step size stays set by α alone.
  • NAdam adds Nesterov's look-ahead to this first moment.

Check yourself

  • From slide 1: which failure of plain SGD does momentum fix? The zig-zag across the steep direction (and minibatch noise). In Adam's averaging form it does not make the flat weight's step any bigger: that is idea 2.

Idea 2: divide each step by that weight's typical gradient

Keep a running average of squared gradients. is the weight's typical gradient size, so comes out about the same size for every weight.

Rare features still learn

A rare word's embedding gets a gradient only now and then, so its stays small. When a gradient does arrive, the step is full-size.

Scale-free

Multiply the loss by 1,000: and both grow 1,000×, and the step does not change. SGD's step would grow 1,000×.

Name check

This idea alone is RMSProp (Hinton, 2012). Adam = RMSProp + momentum + a bias correction (next slide).

Steady gradients assumed (m ≈ g, √v ≈ |g|), so the Adam step ≈ α. Real steps vary with noise: slides 5 and 6.

Explain

  • is the root mean square (RMS) of recent gradients for one weight. Dividing by it turns "gradient in loss units" into "how many typical gradients", a unit-free number around ±1.
  • So α becomes a step length in weight units: about how far each weight moves per step, whatever its gradient scale.
  • On the slide-1 valley this is what lets the flat weight w1 move about as fast as the steep weight w2 is allowed to.
  • Why β2 so close to 1? Squared gradients are very noisy (one spike squares into a huge value). A long average keeps the scale estimate stable, so the step size doesn't jump around.

Deeper

  • Lineage: AdaGrad (2011) divides by the root of the sum of all past squared gradients, so its steps shrink forever. RMSProp swaps the sum for a moving average, so the step size can recover. Adam adds momentum on top and corrects the start-up bias.
  • Dividing by is a cheap stand-in for dividing by curvature: a diagonal preconditioner, one number per weight.

Check yourself

  • From slide 2: what does carry that doesn't? The sign (direction). √v is always positive: it only sets the scale.

04 · The algorithm

Adam: two averages, one correction, one update

Everything is per weight: each weight keeps its own and . The correction fixes the fact that both averages start at zero.

Start
1 Gradient
2 Direction
3 Scale
4 Correct
5 Update

Defaults: ( only guards against division by 0)

Why correct? At : and . starts much further below its true size, so and the first step is 3.2× too big. Dividing by gives : a step of exactly .

Chart: constant gradient, β1 0.9, β2 0.999, step size in units of α. Algorithm: Kingma & Ba, "Adam: A Method for Stochastic Optimization", ICLR 2015, Algorithm 1.

Explain the correction

  • Unrolled: m_t = (1−β1)·Σ_{i=1..t} β1^(t−i)·g_i. If the gradients have a steady mean E[g], then E[m_t] = E[g]·(1−β1)·(1 + β1 + … + β1^(t−1)) = E[g]·(1 − β1^t).
  • So m_t is too small by exactly the factor (1 − β1^t). Divide by it and the bias is gone. Same for v_t with g² and β2.
  • β1^t dies fast (0.9^20 ≈ 0.12), β2^t slowly (0.999^1000 ≈ 0.37). That mismatch is why the uncorrected step overshoots for hundreds of steps, not just a few.
  • Without the correction you would need a long, careful warmup. The Adam paper shows training going unstable without it when β2 is close to 1.

Deeper

  • Implementations fold the two corrections into the step size: α_t = α·√(1−β2^t)/(1−β1^t), then θ −= α_t·m_t/(√v_t + ε'). PyTorch computes denom = √v_t/√(1−β2^t) + ε, which equals √v̂_t + ε as on the slide.
  • ε also caps the step for a weight whose gradients are ~0: the ratio can't explode.

Check yourself

  • From slide 3: why is v's start-up bias bigger than m's? β2 = 0.999 is much closer to 1, so the zero start fades over ~1,000 steps instead of ~10.
  • From slide 2: which line would you delete to get RMSProp? Line 2 (use g instead of m), plus the corrections.

Simulated with β1 0.9, β2 0.999, ε 1e-8; 300 steps per stream, last 60 shown. A: 10 + noise (sd 0.5). B: 0.1 + noise (sd 0.005). C: ±5 alternating. D: 0.01 every 50th step, 0 otherwise.

The two moments in plain words

  • First moment m = running mean of the gradient. It answers "which way have I been pushed lately?". Averaging keeps what is consistent and cancels what flips: that is momentum, in EMA form.
  • Second moment v = running mean of the squared gradient. It answers "how hard am I usually pushed?". Squaring throws the sign away, so v only knows size. √v is the gradient's RMS: its typical magnitude.
  • Statistically, v is the uncentered second moment: E[g²] = μ² + σ². temp.py comments call it "variance"; the variance would be v̂ − m̂².

How Adam uses them

  • m̂ goes in the numerator: the direction, already smoothed.
  • √v̂ goes in the denominator: it divides each weight's step by that weight's own typical gradient, so the ratio is unit-free, about ±1 when the gradient is steady.
  • Result, per weight: A and B both move about α per step although their gradients differ 100× (temp.py's "big gradients → smaller steps, small gradients → bigger steps" means exactly this normalisation). C barely moves, because m̂ cancels while √v̂ stays large. D's rare, tiny spike still moves the weight about 0.7α, because its √v̂ is small too.

In temp.py

m_buffers[i] and v_buffers[i] hold the two moments per parameter; _update_moments(i, grad) updates them and applies the bias correction; step() uses them in one line: param.data -= lr * m_hat / (np.sqrt(v_hat) + eps).

Check yourself

  • Why can't Adam use v alone to choose the direction? Squaring removes the sign; only m knows which way to go.
  • In case C, what would plain SGD do? Move ±5·lr every step: the zig-zag of slide 1.

06 · Why it works

The step follows the gradient's signal-to-noise ratio

is the average gradient (signal); is its typical size (signal and noise together). When gradients agree, the ratio is near 1. When they are mostly noise, it is small.

gradient mean , spread

Clear direction: a full step

Consistent gradients give , so the weight moves about .

Mostly noise: a small step

Near a minimum the gradients are mostly noise, so the steps shrink on their own. Kingma & Ba call this automatic annealing.

So α is a distance

Each weight moves at most about per step (worst case with the default betas). That is why is a sane default, and fine-tuning uses to .

Simulated: gradient = μ + noise (σ = 1), 4,000 Adam steps per point, default betas, mean |m̂/√v̂| after step 500. At μ = 0 the step is 0.19α, not 0: m̂ itself still carries some noise.

Explain

  • √v̂ estimates √E[g²] = √(μ² + σ²): the gradient's size including its noise. m̂ estimates μ. Their ratio is a signal-to-noise measure between 0 and about 1.
  • This is why Adam is robust: the step is driven by how sure the gradients are about the direction, not by how large they are (slide 3: scale-free).
  • Automatic annealing is partial: noise in m̂ keeps a floor (0.19α at zero signal here). That is why a learning-rate schedule that decays α is still used.

Deeper: the bound

  • Kingma & Ba (section 2.1): |step| ≤ α·(1−β1)/√(1−β2) when 1−β1 > √(1−β2), else ≤ α. With 0.9 / 0.999 that is 0.1/0.0316 ≈ 3.2α: the case of one sudden big gradient after a long quiet stretch. Typical steps are ≤ α.
  • Because α is a distance in weight space, you can reason about it directly: "how far can a weight drift in 1,000 steps?" is at most about 1,000·α.

Check yourself

  • From slide 4: without the bias correction, what would this chart show for the first ~100 steps? Steps 3–6.6× too big, whatever the signal-to-noise.

07 · In practice

In practice: use AdamW, and know what it costs

The whole optimizer is six lines. What matters in real training is weight decay, the learning rate, and memory.

# one AdamW step, per weight tensor p (t starts at 1)
p -= lr * wd * p              # AdamW: decay first
m = b1 * m + (1 - b1) * g     # direction
v = b2 * v + (1 - b2) * g * g # scale
m_hat = m / (1 - b1 ** t)     # bias correction
v_hat = v / (1 - b2 ** t)
p -= lr * m_hat / (np.sqrt(v_hat) + eps)

# the same, in PyTorch
opt = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(),
    lr=1e-3, betas=(0.9, 0.999), eps=1e-8,
    weight_decay=0.01)

AdamW, not Adam + L2

With L2, the decay term is added to and then divided by , so weights with big gradients barely decay. AdamW shrinks weights directly, outside the adaptive step (Loshchilov & Hutter, 2019).

Learning rate and warmup

from scratch; to to fine-tune a transformer. Large pretraining often lowers to 0.95–0.98. A short warmup is standard: early rests on few gradients.

Memory: 2 extra numbers per weight

and double the model's size in optimizer state. Your 784 → 256 → 128 → 10 MLP (235,146 weights): +1.9 MB in float32. roberta-base (125M): about 1 GB.

In your optimizers.py

Same shape as your SGD: per-parameter state lists for and (like momentum_buffers, indexed by [i]), from step_count + 1, gradients from _extract_gradient().

Kingma & Ba, ICLR 2015; Loshchilov & Hutter, "Decoupled Weight Decay Regularization", ICLR 2019. PyTorch AdamW applies the decay before the moment updates, as in the code.

Explain

  • Why AdamW matters. L2 regularization adds λθ to the loss, so λθ lands in g. Adam then divides it by √v: a weight with large gradients has a large √v, so its decay gets divided away. Decoupled decay (p -= lr·wd·p) treats every weight the same. With SGD the two are equivalent; with Adam they are not.
  • In your framework. src/core/optimizers.py already has what Adam needs: Optimizer.params, step_count (use t = step_count + 1 so the bias correction never divides by 0), _extract_gradient() and the skip for param.grad is None. Keep one m and one v buffer per parameter, created lazily with np.zeros_like(param.data).
  • Watch the indexing. Your SGD momentum bug (line 260) is grad_data = self.momentum_buffers instead of [i]. Adam has two such buffer lists, so the same slip is twice as likely.
  • Adam vs AdamW in your code. Your SGD adds weight_decay * param.data to the gradient (L2). For Adam that is the coupled version; AdamW instead does param.data -= lr * wd * param.data before the moment updates.
  • Memory. fp32 training holds weights + gradients + m + v = 4 copies of the model. Options when that hurts: Adafactor (factored v; already in your config's optimizer list), 8-bit Adam, or sharding the state (ZeRO/FSDP).

Known limits

  • On some vision tasks, SGD + momentum generalizes better than adaptive methods (Wilson et al., 2017). For transformers, AdamW is the standard.
  • Adam can fail to converge on specially built convex problems (Reddi et al., 2018, AMSGrad). Rare in practice.
  • Mixed precision: keep m and v in fp32 (AMP does this); ε = 1e-8 is below fp16's smallest normal number.

Check yourself

  • From slide 6: why does a fine-tuning lr of 5e-5 make sense for a pretrained model? α is roughly how far each weight moves per step. Small α keeps the pretrained weights close to where they started.
  • From slide 3: why does L2 inside Adam under-regularize weights with big gradients? Their √v is large, and the decay term gets divided by it.
